context_blurb:
A chemical equation writes a reaction as a sum: reactants, the substances going in, left of the arrow; products on the right. Since a reaction never makes or destroys atoms, both sides must hold the same ones. Then a second puzzle: why does rust creep while a dust cloud explodes?

Balancing changes only the coefficients, the big numbers in front; a formula's small numbers, its subscripts, fix what substance it is. The Space Shuttle's main engines joined liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen into water, but H2 + O2 → H2O loses an oxygen atom. Balanced, it reads 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, with four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms on each side. H2O2 would even the count too, but it is hydrogen peroxide.

For Fritz Haber's ammonia, 2NH3 on the right holds six hydrogen atoms. Each H2 molecule brings two hydrogen atoms, so a 3 goes in front of H2, giving N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. A 6 would count atoms, not molecules. Made over hot iron, his ammonia now fertilises the crops that feed about half the world's people and won him the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The same Haber oversaw Germany's first large chlorine gas attack, at Ypres in April 1915, and is called the father of chemical warfare.

A metal such as zinc, magnesium or iron fizzes in an acid, giving off hydrogen and leaving a salt dissolved, such as zinc chloride. Hydrogen burns, so a lit splint at the mouth of its tube goes off with a squeaky pop, the classic test. Acid on marble makes a gas that puts a splint out; oxygen, which does not burn, only makes a glowing splint flare.

A base, such as sodium hydroxide, is an acid's chemical opposite, and neutralising one with the other makes new substances rather than merely diluting both. The acid's hydrogen ions, charged particles, join the base's hydroxide ions as water. With hydrochloric acid and just enough sodium hydroxide, the leftover sodium and chloride form sodium chloride, so the flask holds only a salt and water.

Rust is iron joined with oxygen and water; three nails show that both are needed. One lies in water boiled free of air, under oil that keeps air out. That nail has water but no oxygen and stays bright, so water with no oxygen cannot rust iron. A second, in air kept dry by calcium chloride, stays bright too, ruling out oxygen alone. Only the nail in open water, with air above, rusts.

Particles react only when they collide with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy. Ten degrees of warming roughly doubles many reactions' rates, yet in a gas going from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius the particles meet under two percent more often. Warming greatly raises the number of fast, energetic particles, so many more of the collisions carry enough energy to react. The minimum itself stays put.

Crowding particles closer also speeds a reaction: fire needs oxygen molecules to strike its fuel, and only a fifth of air is oxygen. On 27 January 1967, in a launch-pad test, Roger Chaffee, Ed White and Gus Grissom were sealed in their Apollo 1 capsule in pure oxygen. A spark, most likely electrical, lit nylon and foam, fire filled the cabin within half a minute, and the three astronauts died. Pure oxygen packs about five times as many oxygen molecules into each litre as air, so far more strike the fuel every second. NASA afterwards launched crews in 60 percent oxygen, 40 percent nitrogen.

Surface matters too, because burning happens only where a fuel's surface meets oxygen. In a heap of sawdust, air reaches only the specks on top, so the heap just smoulders. Blown into a cloud, each flying speck meets the air all round, so the whole surface of every speck burns at once. In 1878 a spark lit flour dust in the air of the Washburn A Mill in Minneapolis, and the blast and fire killed 18 people.

A catalyst speeds a reaction without being used up, by offering a route with a lower activation energy. Hydrogen peroxide slowly splits into water and oxygen by itself; a pinch of manganese dioxide makes it froth in seconds. A reactant is used up as it turns into products, so if the powder were one, less of it would be left after the frothing. Filtered, washed and dried, the manganese dioxide weighs just what it did and sets fresh peroxide frothing: a catalyst.
